# Where we are

Weeks 4 and 5 were about whether your **variable** means what you think it means.

--

<br>

Today is about whether your **comparison** means what you think it means.

--

<br>

This is the oldest problem in the course and the one your field has thought hardest
about. It is also the one AI has quietly made worse.

---

# Table of contents

1. [The credibility problem, restated](#credibility)

2. [Specification search](#spec)

3. [Pre-registration](#prereg)

4. [Observational designs](#observational)

5. [Experiments](#experiments)

6. [Nulls and publication bias](#nulls)

7. [Provenance and fraud](#provenance)

8. [Journals and the process](#journals)

9. [Where this leaves you](#close)

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: credibility

# The credibility problem, restated

---

# The question for today

.large2[If a hundred specifications cost nothing to run, what does a reported
specification mean?]

--

<br>

Sit with that for a second. It is not rhetorical.

---

# What the credibility revolution assumed

Angrist, Imbens, Card, Krueger. Design over modeling. Identification over functional
form.

--

<br>

That literature solved a real problem, and your econometrics sequence is downstream of
it.

--

<br>

But it carried an implicit assumption that nobody wrote down.

---

# The implicit assumption

Running a specification was **expensive**.

--

You had to write the code. Debug the merge. Wait for it to run. Build the table by hand.

--

<br>

So researchers ran a handful. Maybe a few dozen over a project's life.

--

<br>

The published specification was a draw from a small set. Not a random draw, nobody
thought that. But a small set.

---

# That assumption is gone

I can ask a model for 500 specifications and have them in an afternoon.

--

Every combination of controls. Every fixed-effects structure. Every sample restriction.
Every winsorization threshold. Every clustering level.

--

<br>

Formatted into a nice table. With stars.

--

<br>

The garden of forking paths is now a paved highway with signage.

---

# The arithmetic

Suppose 12 binary analyst decisions: include controls or not, log or level, drop
outliers or not, cluster here or there.

--

$2^{12} = 4{,}096$ specifications.

--

<br>

Under a true null with independent tests, the probability that **none** hits $p < .05$ is
essentially zero.

--

They are not independent, so it is not literally $4{,}096$ shots. But it is not one
shot either.

--

<br>

And you do not have to run all of them to be in trouble. You only have to *stop* when
you like the answer.

---

# The honest version

Nobody in this room sits down and decides to p-hack.

--

<br>

What happens is: the first specification gives a null. You think, "the controls are
wrong." You fix them. Now it works. You move on.

--

Every step is defensible. The sequence is not.

--

<br>

.large2[Specification search does not feel like cheating. It feels like doing your job.]

---

# What changed is the surface area

Every classical concern about specification search is now worse by roughly an order of
magnitude.

--

- More specifications, faster
- Less friction to stop when you like the result
- No paper trail, unless you build one
- A new dimension: the **prompt**

--

<br>

The profession has not caught up. Journal norms, referee checklists, and your training
were all built for a world where running a regression took a week.

--

That world is over. The norms have not moved.

---

# So this lecture is defensive

Not "here are the identification strategies". You have had that course.

--

<br>

This is: **what does a referee attack, and what do you build so that it survives?**

--

<br>

You are all going to be referees in about three years. Learn the attacks from both
sides.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: spec

# Specification search

---

# The demonstration

.small90[Simmons, Nelson & Simonsohn (2011), "False-Positive Psychology: Undisclosed
Flexibility in Data Collection and Analysis Allows Presenting Anything as Significant,"
*Psychological Science* 22(11):1359–1366.]

--

<br>

They ran an actual experiment and reported that listening to "When I'm Sixty-Four"
made subjects **younger**.

--

$p < .05$. Real data. Real subjects.

---

# How they did it

Four "researcher degrees of freedom," each individually unremarkable:

--

1. Two dependent variables, report the one that works
2. Add 10 more observations if $p$ is close
3. Control for gender, or interact with it
4. Drop one of three conditions

--

<br>

Each is a decision an honest researcher makes. Together, the false-positive rate goes
from 5% to over 60%.

--

<br>

That is the whole paper, and it changed a field.

---

# The generalization

Any single analytic choice is defensible.

--

The **choice of which choices to report** is the entire problem.

--

<br>

.large2[Flexibility alone gets you to $p < .05$ on nonsense.]

You do not need bad intent. You need degrees of freedom and a preference for results.

---

# Does this happen in economics?

.small90[Brodeur, Cook & Heyes (2020), "Methods Matter: p-Hacking and Publication Bias
in Causal Analysis in Economics," *American Economic Review* 110(11):3634–3660.]

--

<br>

They collect tens of thousands of test statistics from top economics journals and look
at the **distribution** of $z$-statistics.

---

# The logic of the z-curve

Under a mix of true nulls and true effects, the density of $z$-statistics should be
smooth.

--

<br>

What you actually see is a **hole just below** the conventional threshold and a **spike
just above** it.

--

<br>

Missing marginal nulls. Excess marginal significance.

--

That shape does not arise from nature. It arises from choices, by authors, referees,
and editors.

---

# The finding that should worry you

They break it out by method.

--

<br>

**Worst:** instrumental variables (**IV**)

**Also problematic, but less so:** difference-in-differences (**DiD**)

**Better:** randomized controlled trials (**RCT**), regression discontinuity (**RDD**)

--

<br>

.small90[I will use those four abbreviations for the rest of the day.]

--

<br>

Read this alongside the published Comment: **Kranz & Pütz (2022)**, *AER* 112(9):3124-3136,
find that after correcting for rounding, the evidence of p-hacking **vanishes for DiD**
while remaining for IV. Reply at 112(9):3137-3139.

--

<br>

This is not a statement about which methods are *valid*. It is a statement about how
much **latitude** each one gives you.

---

# Why IV and DiD are p-hackable

**IV:** which instrument, which first stage, which controls, which sample. Weak
instruments make estimates enormously sensitive to all of it. And there is no test of
the exclusion restriction to discipline you.

--

**DiD:** which comparison group, which window, which fixed effects, which clustering,
which event-time normalization.

--

<br>

**RCT and RDD** are harder to torture because the design pins down more of the analysis
before you see the outcome.

--

<br>

That is the lesson: *design constrains you*, and being constrained is a feature.

---

# Multiple hypothesis testing

The mechanical version of the same problem. You have $k$ outcomes, or $k$ subgroups, or
$k$ treatment arms.

--

<br>

Test each at $\alpha = .05$ and your probability of at least one false positive is not
$.05$.

--

With 12 independent tests under the null: $1 - .95^{12} \approx 0.46$.

--

<br>

Coin-flip odds that something in your table is spurious.

---

# Two things you might want to control

**Family-wise error rate (FWER)**: probability of *any* false rejection.

Conservative. Appropriate when a single false claim is costly, one confirmatory
outcome, a regulatory decision, a policy recommendation.

--

<br>

**False discovery rate (FDR)**: expected *proportion* of rejections that are false.

Less conservative. Appropriate for screening. You are generating hypotheses, and some
false leads are tolerable.

--

<br>

These answer different questions. Pick the one that matches what you are claiming.

---

# The two procedures you need

**Bonferroni.** Compare each $p$-value to $\alpha/k$. Controls FWER. Simple, valid
always, and brutally conservative when tests are correlated.

--

**Benjamini–Hochberg.** Sort $p_{(1)} \le \dots \le p_{(k)}$; find the largest $i$ with
$p_{(i)} \le \frac{i}{k}\alpha$; reject everything up to it. Controls FDR.

--

<br>

Also worth knowing: **Romano–Wolf** step-down, which bootstraps the joint distribution
and exploits correlation across outcomes. Much more powerful than Bonferroni when your
outcomes are related, which they usually are. Implemented in Stata and R.

---

# When do you actually need to correct?

**Yes:** many outcomes, many subgroups, many arms, and you are claiming *any* of them
as a finding.

--

**Yes:** heterogeneity analysis where you searched over splits.

--

<br>

**Not really:** one pre-specified primary outcome. That is the point of having one.

--

**Not really:** a robustness table where every column is estimating the *same*
parameter. Those are not $k$ hypotheses; they are one hypothesis probed $k$ ways.

--

<br>

That distinction confuses people constantly. Robustness $\ne$ multiplicity.

---

# The practical version

.large2[If you have 12 outcomes, you have a problem, and the referee will notice.]

--

<br>

Your options:

1. Name **one** primary outcome in advance and treat the rest as exploratory, labeled
2. Build a pre-specified **index** of related outcomes and test that
3. Report adjusted $p$-values alongside raw ones

--

<br>

What you cannot do is report 12 outcomes, star the three that worked, and write the
abstract about those three. A good referee catches this in ten minutes.

---

# Specification curve analysis

The partial remedy: stop picking.

--

<br>

Enumerate the set of defensible specifications. Run all of them. Plot the whole
distribution of estimates, sorted, with the analytic choices displayed underneath.

--

<br>

Also called **multiverse analysis**. Same idea.

---

# What it buys you

If your effect is there in 480 of 500 defensible specifications, that is a much stronger
claim than one table.

--

<br>

If it is there in 60 of 500, you have learned something too. And you now have an
obligation to say so.

--

<br>

Note that this is exactly the kind of thing that is now trivially cheap to produce. The
same capability that makes p-hacking easy makes the honest version easy.

---

# Where it can be gamed

.large2[Who decides which specifications are "defensible"?]

--

<br>

You do. And the set is chosen after you know which ones work.

--

<br>

A specification curve computed over a set curated to include your preferred spec and
exclude its enemies is a p-hacked specification curve with better graphics.

--

I have refereed papers where this happened. It is not obvious from the figure.

---

# So how do you make it credible?

- Define the specification set **before** running it, and say so
- Include the specifications a *hostile* referee would demand, not the ones you like
- Show the distribution, not just "most are significant"
- Report the fraction with the wrong sign, and the median, not just the mode

--

<br>

If a skeptic would have drawn the same set you did, the curve is informative. If not, it
is decoration.

---

# Callback to Week 4

Remember what we said about prompts.

--

<br>

You wrote a prompt. It gave you 71% accuracy. You rewrote it. 78%. You added few-shot
examples. 84%. You changed the label taxonomy. 88%.

--

<br>

.large2[Prompt search **is** specification search.]

--

Same problem. New surface. And unlike regression specifications, nobody has a norm for
reporting it yet.

---

# Why the prompt case is worse

With regressions, at least the specification is *visible* in the paper.

--

<br>

With prompts:

- The search happens in a chat window with no log
- The intermediate versions are not saved
- The paper reports one prompt, in an appendix, with no history
- And if you tuned the prompt while watching the **downstream** coefficient, you have
  p-hacked through a measurement instrument

--

<br>

That last one is the bad case, and it is easy to do by accident.

---

# The rule for your project

Tune the prompt against **validation accuracy**, on a held-out validation sample.

--

Never against the downstream estimate.

--

<br>

Freeze the prompt before you look at the regression. Version it in `prompts/`. Log the
iterations in `ai-log.md`.

--

<br>

This is why I made you keep those directories in Week 1. This is the slide where that
pays off.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: prereg

# Pre-registration

---

# The idea

Researcher degrees of freedom are not the problem. **Undisclosed** researcher degrees of
freedom are the problem.

--

<br>

.large2[Pre-registration converts degrees of freedom into a commitment device.]

--

<br>

You state, in a timestamped public document, what you will do before you do it.

---

# What a pre-analysis plan contains

- The hypotheses, stated as testable propositions
- The **primary** outcome. Singular, ideally
- Secondary and exploratory outcomes, labeled as such
- The estimating equation, including controls and fixed effects
- The sample and exclusion rules
- The clustering level
- The multiplicity correction, if any
- The power calculation and target $N$
- The stopping rule

---

# What it does not do

**It does not ban exploration.**

This is the most common misreading. You can explore all you want. You are required to
*label* it.

--

<br>

Confirmatory results carry the pre-specified error rate. Exploratory results are
hypothesis generation.

--

Both belong in the paper. They are just different claims.

---

# What it genuinely does not fix

**It does not make a bad design good.** A pre-registered study with a confounded
comparison is a pre-registered confounded comparison.

--

<br>

**Plans are often vague enough to be unbinding.** "We will estimate the effect of the
treatment on engagement, controlling for relevant covariates." That constrains nothing.

--

<br>

**It is awkward for observational work.** The data already exist. You have probably
already looked at them. Pre-registering after the fact is theater.

---

# The observational case, honestly

Most of what you will do in marketing is observational. Pre-registration in its pure
form does not apply.

--

<br>

What *does* transfer:

- Write the identification argument **before** the results
- Specify the primary specification before running the alternatives
- Commit to the robustness checks in advance, including the ones you fear
- Hold out a portion of the data, or a later time period, if the design permits

--

<br>

The mechanism you want is a commitment made before you learn the answer. A registry is
one way to get it. Not the only way.

---

# For your project specifically

.large2[Pre-specify the prompt and the primary specification before looking at any
downstream result.]

--

<br>

Write it in your repo. Commit it. Timestamp it with git.

--

That commit hash is your pre-registration. It is not public, and it is not a registry,
but it is a real commitment and I can check it.

--

<br>

If your Week 6 milestone specification differs from what you present in Week 7, tell me
why. That is a fine thing to have happen. Hiding it is not.

---

# Registries

**AEA RCT Registry**, `socialscienceregistry.org`. Standard for field experiments in
economics. Required by many funders and increasingly expected by editors.

--

**OSF**, `osf.io`. General purpose, flexible, widely used in psychology and marketing.

--

**AsPredicted**, `aspredicted.org`. Nine questions, short, low friction. Good for lab
and online experiments. The low friction is the point: a plan you actually write beats
a perfect plan you don't.

--

<br>

All are free. All take under an hour for a simple experiment.

---

# Norms in marketing

Weaker than in psychology. Weaker than in development or experimental economics.

--

<br>

Marketing Science and JMR do not require pre-registration for experimental work.
Reviewers increasingly ask.

--

<br>

This is changing, and it is changing in one direction. Registered reports are appearing.
Data availability policies have tightened.

--

<br>

You are entering the field at the point where the norm shifts. Being early costs you
almost nothing and will look prescient in five years.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: observational

# Observational designs

### What survives a referee

---

# The four questions

You have seen these since Lecture 1. Here they are as a referee uses them.

--

1. **What is the estimand?** What number are you trying to learn, for whom?

2. **What is the identifying assumption?** What has to be true for your estimate to be
   that number?

3. **What would break it?** Name the violation.

4. **What is the most damaging alternative explanation?** Not a generic one. The
   specific story a smart skeptic tells.

--

<br>

If you cannot answer all four about your own project by Week 7, you are not ready to
present.

---

# On question 4 specifically

Most papers I referee answer questions 1–3 and skip 4.

--

<br>

Question 4 is the one that decides the paper.

--

<br>

.large2[Write down the best argument against your result, in its strongest form, and
then address it.]

--

If you write a weak version of the objection and knock it down, every referee sees what
you did.

---

# Difference-in-differences

The workhorse. Treated and control units, before and after.

--

**Identifying assumption:** parallel trends. Absent treatment, the two groups' outcomes
would have moved in parallel.

--

<br>

Note what this is *not*: it is not that the groups are similar. Levels can differ
arbitrarily. It is a statement about **counterfactual trends**, which are unobservable.

--

<br>

That is why it can never be tested. Only made more or less plausible.

---

# What the referee attacks in DiD

- Why is this control group the right counterfactual?
- What else happened at the same time to the treated group?
- Is treatment timing correlated with the outcome's trajectory? (Ashenfelter dips.)
- Is anticipation contaminating the pre-period?
- Are there spillovers from treated to control units?

--

<br>

And, since about 2021, one more that will get your paper rejected if you have not
addressed it.

---

# Staggered adoption

If units adopt treatment at **different times** and you run two-way fixed effects with a
single treatment dummy, you need to know what you have actually estimated.

--

<br>

.large2[It is not the average treatment effect on the treated.]

--

<br>

Three papers made this unavoidable. You need all three.

---

# Goodman-Bacon (2021)

.small90["Difference-in-Differences with Variation in Treatment Timing," *Journal of
Econometrics* 225(2):254–277.]

--

<br>

The decomposition. **TWFE**, two-way fixed effects, the unit-and-time fixed effects
regression you have written a hundred times, with staggered timing is a **weighted
average of all possible 2×2 DiD comparisons**.

--

Including comparisons of **later-treated to already-treated** units.

--

<br>

In those comparisons, the already-treated unit serves as a control. So its own ongoing
treatment effect enters with the **wrong sign**.

---

# Why that matters

If treatment effects are constant across units and time, the bad comparisons wash out.
Fine.

--

<br>

If treatment effects are **heterogeneous**, different across cohorts, or dynamic over
time. They do not.

--

<br>

You can get a TWFE estimate with the **opposite sign** from every unit-level effect in
your data.

--

<br>

Not a small bias. A sign flip.

---

# de Chaisemartin & D'Haultfœuille (2020)

.small90["Two-Way Fixed Effects Estimators with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects,"
*American Economic Review* 110(9):2964–2996.]

--

<br>

Makes the weights explicit and shows they can be **negative**.

--

<br>

They provide a diagnostic: compute the weights for your own specification and report
how many are negative and how much mass they carry.

--

<br>

Run it. It takes minutes. If your negative weights are large, your TWFE estimate is not
interpretable and you need a different estimator.

---

# Callaway & Sant'Anna (2021)

.small90["Difference-in-Differences with Multiple Time Periods," *Journal of
Econometrics* 225(2):200–230.]

--

<br>

The fix. Estimate group-time average treatment effects $ATT(g,t)$, one for each
adoption cohort $g$ and period $t$, using **clean** comparisons only (never-treated or
not-yet-treated units).

--

Then aggregate deliberately: by cohort, by calendar time, or by event time.

--

<br>

The aggregation is now your choice, made explicit, rather than a weighting scheme the
regression imposed on you without telling you.

---

# What this means for you

.large2[TWFE with staggered timing and heterogeneous effects is not what you think it
is.]

--

<br>

If your design has staggered adoption:

- Report the Goodman-Bacon decomposition or the negative-weight diagnostic
- Report a robust estimator (Callaway–Sant'Anna, or one of the others in this
  literature) alongside TWFE
- If they differ, that is a **finding**, not an inconvenience

--

<br>

A referee who knows this literature (and by now that is most of them) will ask. Do it
before they do.

---

# Event studies

Plot coefficients on leads and lags of treatment. The standard visual.

--

<br>

Two things it does:

1. Shows **dynamics**, does the effect grow, decay, or appear immediately?
2. Shows **pre-trends**, were the groups diverging before treatment?

--

<br>

The second is why everyone puts one in the paper.

---

# The limits of pre-trend tests

Flat pre-trends are reassuring. They are **not** proof of parallel counterfactual
trends.

--

<br>

Three reasons:

--

**Power.** Pre-treatment coefficients are often imprecise. "Not significantly different
from zero" with wide confidence intervals is not evidence of anything.

--

**Selection on the test.** If you chose the comparison group partly because the
pre-trends looked flat, the test is no longer informative. You conditioned on passing
it.

--

**Timing.** A confounder that switches on exactly at treatment leaves no pre-trend at
all.

---

# How to use event studies well

- Plot the coefficients **with confidence intervals**, always. Never just point
  estimates.
- State the normalization period explicitly. It is a choice and it matters.
- Ask whether your pre-period is **powered** to detect a trend large enough to matter
- Treat a flat pre-trend as one piece of evidence, not as the identification argument

--

<br>

The identification argument is a **substantive** claim about why treatment timing is
unrelated to the outcome's path. The event study supports it. It is not a substitute for
it.

---

# Instrumental variables

Need: relevance ($Z$ moves $D$) and the **exclusion restriction** ($Z$ affects $Y$ only
through $D$).

--

<br>

Relevance is testable. Look at the first stage.

--

<br>

.large2[The exclusion restriction is an assumption, not a test.]

--

<br>

Overidentification tests do not test it. They test whether your instruments agree with
each other. Instruments can be jointly invalid in the same direction and sail through.

---

# Weak instruments

A weak first stage is not merely imprecise. It is **biased toward OLS**, and the bias is
worst exactly when you needed IV most.

--

<br>

The old $F > 10$ rule of thumb is too permissive. The current standard is
Montiel Olea–Pflueger effective $F$, or Anderson–Rubin confidence sets, which are valid
regardless of instrument strength.

--

<br>

If your first-stage $F$ is 12, do not report 2SLS standard errors as if they were
correct. Report an AR confidence set.

---

# The clever instrument trap

You know the genre. Rainfall. Distance to something. A historical accident. Something
from the 1800s.

--

<br>

The instrument is surprising, and the surprise reads as credibility.

--

<br>

.large2[Cleverness is not validity.]

--

The right question is never "is this instrument clever?" It is: **through what other
channel could this variable affect the outcome?**

--

If rainfall affects income and income affects your outcome directly, the instrument is
dead no matter how novel it is.

---

# How to defend an IV

- State the exclusion restriction in **words**, as a substantive claim about the world
- Enumerate the alternative channels and address each one specifically
- Show the reduced form. If the reduced form is noise, your IV estimate is a ratio of
  noise to a small number
- Report first-stage strength honestly
- Say what the **LATE** is: whose behavior does the instrument move? That is the
  population your estimate describes, and it is often not the one you care about

---

# Regression discontinuity

The most credible observational design when it is available. Assignment is determined by
a running variable crossing a threshold, and units cannot precisely control their
position.

--

<br>

**Identifying assumption:** potential outcomes are continuous at the cutoff. Everything
else about you changes smoothly; only treatment jumps.

---

# What the referee attacks in RDD

**Bandwidth.** Results that appear at one bandwidth and vanish at another are not
results. Report a sensitivity curve. Use a data-driven bandwidth (Calonico–Cattaneo–
Titiunik) rather than one you picked.

--

**Functional form.** Local linear with a sensible kernel. High-order global polynomials
produce artifacts at boundaries, this is well documented and referees know it.

--

**Manipulation.** McCrary density test. If the running variable bunches at the cutoff,
someone is sorting, and continuity fails.

--

**Covariate smoothness.** Predetermined characteristics should not jump at the cutoff.
If they do, something else changes there too.

---

# And the thing people forget

.large2[RDD is **local**.]

--

<br>

You have estimated an effect for units near the threshold. That is the estimand. Not the
average effect in the population.

--

<br>

That is often fine, sometimes the threshold is exactly where policy operates. But you
must say it, and you must not write an abstract that implies otherwise.

--

<br>

Referees are unforgiving about external-validity overreach in RDD papers.

---

# Matching and selection on observables

You match on covariates, or control for them, and claim conditional independence.

--

<br>

**Identifying assumption:** conditional on $X$, treatment is as good as random.

--

<br>

This assumption is enormous, untestable, and usually false.

---

# The sentence that will not survive

> "We control for firm size, industry, and year fixed effects."

--

<br>

.large2["I controlled for it" is not an identification strategy.]

--

<br>

Adding covariates addresses confounding **only** by variables you observed and measured
correctly. The confounders you should worry about are the ones not in your data, and
they are exactly the ones you cannot control for.

--

Adding more controls does not converge to causality. It converges to a more precisely
estimated correlation.

---

# When selection on observables is defensible

It sometimes is. The conditions:

--

- You can articulate the **assignment mechanism** and argue $X$ captures it
- You have rich covariates that plausibly span the selection process
- The remaining variation has a story you can tell
- You bound the problem: sensitivity analysis for unobserved confounding (Oster's
  $\delta$, Rosenbaum bounds) rather than asserting there is none

--

<br>

What is not defensible is running the regression, adding controls until the coefficient
stabilizes, and calling stability identification. Coefficient stability under controls
you chose is weak evidence at best.

---

# Placebo and falsification tests

The most useful robustness you can run, and the most under-used.

--

<br>

The logic: find a setting where your mechanism predicts **no effect**, and show there is
none.

--

<br>

- Outcomes the treatment should not touch
- Units that should not be affected
- Timing shifted to a period before treatment
- Groups ineligible for the policy

--

<br>

A placebo that fails is far more informative than another significant coefficient.

---

# What a real robustness section looks like

Each check gets:

1. A sentence stating **the concern**: "To address the concern that treated markets
   were already on a different trajectory..."
2. The check
3. The result, including when it is weaker

--

<br>

Not: a table of 14 columns with no explanation and a sentence saying results are robust.

--

<br>

.large2[If a robustness check cannot fail, it is not a check.]

--

Ask yourself, before running each one: what result would make me abandon the claim? If
the answer is "nothing," delete the table.

---

# Clustering

.large2[Cluster at the level of treatment assignment.]

--

<br>

If treatment varies at the state level, cluster at the state level, even if you have
millions of individual observations.

--

Individual-level clustering with state-level treatment gives you standard errors that
are too small by a large factor. This is Moulton, it is thirty years old, and people
still get it wrong.

---

# Few clusters

The asymptotics that justify cluster-robust standard errors are in the **number of
clusters**, not observations.

--

<br>

With 10 or 15 clusters, cluster-robust standard errors over-reject substantially. Your
$t$-statistics are inflated.

--

<br>

Remedies: wild cluster bootstrap (Cameron–Gelbach–Miller), randomization inference, or
$t$-distribution critical values with $G-1$ degrees of freedom.

--

<br>

If you have 12 states and you report standard clustered SEs, a referee will ask. Have
the bootstrap ready.

---

# Two clustering mistakes I see constantly

**1. Clustering at a level finer than assignment** because it gives smaller standard
errors and someone told you to cluster at the "most granular" level. Wrong direction.

--

**2. Clustering on the LLM-measured variable's unit** and forgetting that measurement
error from a *shared* prompt is correlated across all observations.

--

<br>

That second one is new and specific to what you are doing. If one prompt annotated your
whole sample, its errors are not independent across observations. That correlation does
not vanish because you clustered on something else.

--

We touched this in Week 5. It belongs in your clustering decision.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: experiments

# Experiments

---

# Why experiments

You control assignment.

--

<br>

.large2[Identification is by design, not by assumption.]

--

<br>

Randomization makes treatment independent of potential outcomes by construction. No
parallel trends. No exclusion restriction. No conditional independence.

--

<br>

This is why RCTs and RDD show the least evidence of p-hacking in Brodeur et al. The
design does the work that specification choices would otherwise have to do.

---

# But experiments have their own failure modes

They are different failure modes, and they are less discussed because the design feels
airtight.

--

<br>

- Peeking and optional stopping
- False discovery across many tests
- Underpowered designs
- Interference between units
- Attrition and non-compliance
- Measuring the wrong thing

--

<br>

Running an experiment does not exempt you from thinking. It changes what you have to
think about.

---

# A/B testing at scale

Every platform runs thousands of experiments a year. Airbnb, Amazon, Meta, Netflix,
Booking.

--

<br>

If you work with industry data, or go to industry, this *is* the empirical environment.

--

<br>

And the environment has a structural problem: enormous numbers of tests, small true
effects, and a decision process that acts on whatever comes back significant.

---

# Peeking

You launch the test. You check it on day 2. Not significant. Day 4. Not significant. Day
6. Significant! Ship it.

--

<br>

.large2[This is not a valid test.]

--

<br>

Fixed-sample $p$-values assume you look **once**, at a pre-specified sample size.

--

Repeatedly testing as data accumulate and stopping at the first significant result
inflates the false-positive rate to well above 5%. Under continuous monitoring with no
correction, it converges toward 1.

---

# The mechanism

The $p$-value path is a random walk. Under the null, it wanders.

--

<br>

If you stop the moment it crosses .05, you are not testing a hypothesis. You are waiting
for a random walk to hit a boundary. And it will, eventually.

--

<br>

Every dashboard that shows a live $p$-value creates this problem. Most experimentation
platforms show a live $p$-value.

---

# What to do instead

**Fix the sample size in advance** and analyze once. Simplest, and correct.

--

**Group sequential designs.** Pre-specified interim looks with adjusted boundaries
(O'Brien–Fleming, Pocock). Standard in clinical trials for forty years.

--

**Always-valid inference.** Sequential $p$-values and confidence sequences that remain
valid under continuous monitoring. This is what the better experimentation platforms
have moved to.

--

<br>

You can monitor continuously. You just cannot use fixed-sample $p$-values while doing
it.

---

# Required reading: false discovery in A/B testing

.small90[**Berman & Van den Bulte (2022), "False Discovery in A/B Testing,"
*Management Science* 68(9):6762–6782.**]

--

<br>

They take a large set of real A/B tests from a commercial experimentation platform and
ask: of the tests declared winners, how many are actually true effects?

---

# The setup

The key insight is that this is a **base rate** problem, not a $p$-value problem.

--

<br>

If most tested ideas have effects near zero (which is what the data show) then the set
of significant results is dominated by false positives, even with correct 5% tests.

--

<br>

This is the same arithmetic as a screening test for a rare disease. Good specificity
plus a low base rate gives you mostly false positives among the positives.

---

# What they find

Substantial false discovery among declared winners in real testing programs.

--

<br>

Compounded by:

- **Optional stopping**, practitioners peek, and platforms encourage it
- **Many variants** tested at once without multiplicity adjustment
- **Selection**, only winners get implemented and remembered

--

<br>

The organizational consequence: a firm running a large A/B program can systematically
ship changes that do nothing, and believe it is improving.

---

# Why I assigned it

Two reasons.

--

<br>

**One:** many of you will work with platform experimentation data, and this is the
correct prior to bring to it.

--

**Two:** it is a clean demonstration that "we ran an experiment" is not the end of the
credibility conversation.

--

<br>

Design solves confounding. It does not solve multiplicity, stopping rules, or base
rates.

---

# Required reading: measuring advertising

.small90[**Johnson, Lewis & Nubbemeyer (2017), "Ghost Ads: Improving the Economics of
Measuring Online Ad Effectiveness," *Journal of Marketing Research* 54(6):867–884.**]

--

<br>

Start with the problem this solves, because the problem is bigger than advertising.

---

# The incrementality problem

Advertising is targeted at people who were already likely to convert.

--

<br>

So the naive comparison, exposed versus unexposed, compares people who wanted the
product to people who did not.

--

<br>

.large2[Observational estimates of ad effectiveness are wildly biased upward.]

--

Not by 10%. By multiples. Lewis and Rao's work on this is the canonical demonstration:
the noise in sales relative to plausible ad effects is so large that observational
methods routinely produce estimates orders of magnitude off.

---

# So run an experiment. What is the control group?

Here is the subtlety.

--

<br>

You want: people who **would have been shown the ad** but were not.

--

<br>

You cannot just withhold ads from a random group and compare. The problem is knowing
*which* control-group users would have been served an ad, because ad delivery depends
on an auction, on competing bids, on targeting, on user behavior at that moment.

--

<br>

Comparing all of the control group to the exposed subset of treatment is comparing the
wrong populations.

---

# The old solution: PSAs

Show the control group a **public service announcement** in the same ad slot.

--

<br>

That identifies who *would* have been served. Now you can compare like with like.

--

<br>

Two problems:

- You **pay** for the PSA impressions. Expensive.
- The PSA itself occupies the slot, which may have its own effects, and you have given
  up the ability to serve a profitable ad there

--

<br>

Correct, and costly enough that firms did not do it.

---

# Ghost ads

The design innovation: run a **second simulated auction** to identify which control-group
users *would have* seen the focal ad. And log that, without ever serving it.

--

<br>

Those users just see whatever the platform would have shown anyway: the slot goes to the
next bidder in the ordinary auction.

--

<br>

.large2[The counterfactual is **logged**, not purchased.]

That is the whole cost saving. You get a valid control group without buying a single
impression for it.

--

<br>

You get the same identification of the would-have-been-exposed population, without
paying for placebo impressions and without giving up the inventory.

---

# Why this is a great paper for you

.large2[The contribution is a **design**, not an estimator.]

--

<br>

They did not find a cleverer way to analyze existing data. They changed what data gets
recorded so the comparison becomes valid.

--

<br>

That is the highest-value move in empirical work, and it is available to you far more
often than you think, especially if you are working with a firm, or building your own
measurement pipeline.

--

<br>

Ask, on your own project: *what could I record that would make this comparison clean?*

---

# Power

Run the power calculation **before** the experiment.

--

<br>

You need: the minimum detectable effect you care about, the outcome's variance, your
$\alpha$, your target power (80% conventionally, and 80% is not generous).

--

<br>

Then solve for $N$.

--

If the required $N$ is larger than what you can get, you have learned something valuable
before spending any money: **do not run this experiment**.

---

# Post-hoc power is not a thing

Computing "observed power" from your realized effect size after the fact is a
monotone transformation of your $p$-value.

--

<br>

It contains no information beyond the $p$-value. It cannot tell you whether a null
result was underpowered.

--

<br>

.large2[If a reviewer asks for post-hoc power, they are wrong, and you should politely
give them a confidence interval instead.]

--

The CI answers the question they actually meant to ask: what effect sizes can you rule
out?

---

# The thing many of you have not internalized

.large2[An underpowered study that finds a significant effect is **more** likely to be
wrong, not less.]

--

<br>

This is counterintuitive and it is arithmetic.

---

# Why

Low power means only large estimates clear significance.

--

<br>

If the true effect is small, the only way your noisy estimate reaches significance is if
noise pushed it far from the truth.

--

<br>

So conditional on significance in an underpowered design:

--

- The estimate is **exaggerated in magnitude**, Type M (magnitude) error
- It has a non-trivial chance of the **wrong sign**, Type S (sign) error

--

<br>

Gelman and Carlin's framing. Their worked examples report exaggeration factors of
**9.7, 25, and 77**.

--

<br>

That last one means a published, statistically significant estimate was **77 times** the
plausible true effect.

---

# The consequence for reading literature

A significant result from a study with $N = 80$ is **weaker** evidence than a null from a
study with $N = 8{,}000$.

--

<br>

Most people read it the other way around.

--

<br>

When you referee, ask about power before you ask about anything else. When you present,
report the minimum detectable effect. It tells the audience what your design could and
could not have found.

---

# Interference and SUTVA

The stable unit treatment value assumption: one unit's treatment does not affect another
unit's outcome.

--

<br>

In a marketplace, this is often just false.

---

# Where it breaks in platform settings

**Two-sided markets.** Treat some buyers with a better ranking algorithm. They book the
good listings. Control-group buyers now face worse inventory. The control group has been
treated, in the wrong direction.

--

**Auctions and budgets.** Treated advertisers bid more, raising prices for control
advertisers. Interference through the price.

--

**Social spillovers.** Treated users tell untreated users.

--

**Supply constraints.** Anything with fixed capacity, hotel rooms, drivers, inventory
creates mechanical interference.

---

# What interference does to your estimate

It biases in a direction you can usually sign, and it is often **large**.

--

<br>

If treatment cannibalizes from control, the difference overstates the true effect
possibly enormously, because you have measured redistribution and called it creation.

--

<br>

A ranking change that moves bookings from listing A to listing B looks like a huge
treatment effect at the listing level and may be **zero** at the platform level.

--

<br>

This is the single most common way platform experiments mislead the firms running them.

---

# Partial remedies

**Cluster randomization.** Randomize at the market, city, or region level so spillovers
are contained within units. Costs you power. You now have as many observations as
clusters.

--

**Switchback designs.** Randomize the whole market on and off over time. Standard in
ride-hailing and delivery.

--

**Two-sided / bipartite randomization.** Randomize on both sides to identify
interference terms.

--

<br>

None is free. All are better than pretending SUTVA holds because you did not want to
think about it.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: nulls

# Nulls and publication bias

---

# The file drawer

Studies that find nothing are less likely to be written up, less likely to be submitted,
less likely to be accepted.

--

<br>

.large2[The published literature is a **biased sample** of the research conducted.]

--

<br>

The bias is toward large effects, and it is toward effects estimated with noise, because
noise is what gets marginal studies over the significance line.

---

# What this does to you

The effect sizes in the literature are **upper bounds**, often badly so.

--

<br>

Consequences you will actually experience:

- Your power calculation, based on published effect sizes, is wrong. You will be
  underpowered.
- Your replication fails and you assume you made a mistake
- Meta-analyses inherit the bias unless they correct for it

--

<br>

This is the mechanism behind the replication crisis. It requires no fraud at all, only
selective publication.

---

# When your effect is not there

It will happen on this project. Seven weeks, a new measurement instrument, a hard
question.

--

<br>

The first thing to determine:

--

.large2[Is it a **precise** zero or an **imprecise** one?]

--

<br>

These are entirely different scientific situations and they get written up differently.

---

# The two cases

**Precise zero.** $\hat\beta = 0.002$, 95% CI $[-0.011, 0.015]$, and the literature
claims effects of 0.15.

You have **ruled out** the effect people believed in. That is a finding. It is
publishable.

--

<br>

**Imprecise zero.** $\hat\beta = 0.002$, 95% CI $[-0.9, 0.9]$.

You have learned nothing. Your data cannot distinguish a huge positive effect from a
huge negative one.

--

<br>

Both have $p > .05$. They have nothing else in common.

---

# So report the interval

Never write "we find no significant effect" and stop.

--

<br>

Write: "the estimate is 0.002, with a 95% confidence interval of $[-0.011, 0.015]$,
ruling out effects larger than 1.5%, an order of magnitude below the estimates in
\[literature\]."

--

<br>

Or: "the estimate is 0.002, but the confidence interval spans $[-0.9, 0.9]$, so the
design cannot distinguish economically meaningful effects of either sign."

--

<br>

The second sentence is not a failure to write. It is the correct report of what you
learned, and honest people write it.

---

# Making a null informative

**Equivalence testing (TOST).** Specify the smallest effect that would matter. Test
whether you can reject effects larger than that in either direction. If you can, you have
established practical equivalence, a positive claim, not an absence.

--

<br>

**Bounds.** Even with an imprecise point estimate you can often bound the parameter
using partial-identification arguments (Manski). "The effect is between X and Y" is a
result.

--

<br>

**Minimum detectable effect.** State what your design could have detected. It converts
"we found nothing" into "we can rule out anything above this."

---

# The framing that gets a null published

Nulls get published when they are **informative about something people believed**.

--

<br>

That requires three things:

1. A design credible enough that people believe the null
2. Precision sufficient to rule out the effect that was claimed
3. A claim in the literature or in practice that your null contradicts

--

<br>

A null from a weak, underpowered design is not a finding. It is an absence of evidence,
and you should say so plainly rather than dress it up.

---

# Callback

.large2[A well-designed project that finds nothing gets a **higher grade** than a badly
identified project that finds something.]

--

<br>

I said this in Lecture 1. We are in Week 6 and some of you are about to find out I
meant it.

--

<br>

If your effect is not there, come to office hours. We will figure out whether it is a
precise zero, and if it is, how to write it. That is a good outcome and I will grade it
as one.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: provenance

# Provenance and fraud

---

# A case study

I want to spend real time on one episode, factually.

--

<br>

Not because fraud is common (it is rare) but because this case illustrates exactly how
the checking mechanisms in our field fail, and what would have caught it.

---

# The paper

"Artificial Intelligence, Scientific Discovery, and Product Innovation" (arXiv:2412.17866),
by a then-doctoral student at MIT.

--

<br>

Circulated widely in late 2024 and into 2025. Reported that the rollout of an AI tool at
a large materials-science lab produced large increases in materials discovery, patenting,
and product innovation.

--

<br>

Rich data. Clean staggered rollout design. Heterogeneous effects by scientist ability.
Well written.

---

# The reception

Widely praised, including by prominent economists, Daron Acemoglu and David Autor among
them.

--

<br>

Presented at seminars. Covered in the press. Circulated as evidence in the debate about
AI and productivity.

--

<br>

It was, for several months, one of the most discussed working papers in economics.

---

# What happened

In May 2025, MIT issued a public statement saying it had **no confidence in the
provenance, reliability, or validity of the data** and in the veracity of the research.

--

<br>

The university requested withdrawal from arXiv. The paper was withdrawn.

--

<br>

Acemoglu and Autor publicly stated they no longer had confidence in the paper and asked
for it to be withdrawn from circulation.

---

# The first teaching point

The result was **plausible**. It was **well-written**. And it confirmed what a lot of
smart people already wanted to believe about AI and productivity.

--

<br>

.large2[That is exactly the configuration in which scrutiny fails.]

--

<br>

We scrutinize hardest what surprises us. A finding that fits the prior gets waved
through, by referees, by seminar audiences, by senior people whose endorsement carries
weight.

--

If the paper had reported that the AI tool did nothing, it would have been picked apart
in the first seminar.

---

# The second teaching point

Nobody could check it.

--

<br>

Not because anyone refused. Because there was nothing to check **with**.

--

- The firm was anonymous
- The data were proprietary
- There was no public pipeline
- There was no replication package

--

<br>

Every reader was evaluating the paper on plausibility, prose, and the author's
institution. Those are the three things that are easiest to get right without a real
result.

---

# What actually surfaced it

Not the referee process. Not the seminar circuit. Not the endorsements.

--

<br>

A computer scientist with domain knowledge of materials science who found the described
setting implausible on technical grounds and raised it with the university.

--

<br>

<br>

That is a thin defense. It is essentially luck.

---

# The third teaching point

.large2[Reproducible pipelines and documented provenance are not bureaucratic overhead.]

--

<br>

They are the **mechanism** by which a field can check anything at all.

--

<br>

Every requirement in this course that felt like busywork, raw data read-only, scripted
transformations, versioned prompts, logged model calls, a repo that runs from a clean
clone, exists so that checking is *possible*.

--

Not so that someone will definitely check. So that they *could*.

---

# The question

.large2[If someone asked for your project's raw data and pipeline tomorrow, could you
hand it over. And would it run?]

--

<br>

Be honest with yourself about the answer.

--

<br>

"Would it run" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. Most projects fail on that half,
not the first half.

---

# To be clear about scope

The vast majority of results that do not replicate involve **no fraud whatsoever**.

--

<br>

Specification search. Underpowered designs. Publication bias. Coding errors. Silent
merge failures. A model that dropped 40% of the sample.

--

<br>

Everything in the first half of this lecture, and everything in Week 2.

--

<br>

The infrastructure that catches fraud is the same infrastructure that catches your
honest mistakes. You are building it primarily for the honest mistakes, which are yours,
and which are certain.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: journals

# Journals and the process

---

# Data availability policies

Norms have tightened substantially, and are still tightening.

--

<br>

**AEA journals:** mandatory data and code deposit, verified by a data editor before
publication. They actually run your code.

--

**Management Science, Marketing Science, JMR:** data and code policies in place, with
varying enforcement. Increasingly requested at acceptance.

--

<br>

Proprietary data complicate this. They do not exempt you. The expectation is that you
deposit code, document access procedures, and provide enough for someone to replicate
with equivalent data.

---

# What this means practically

.large2[Build the replication package as you go, not at acceptance.]

--

<br>

The alternative is reconstructing, eighteen months later, what you did to a dataset you
no longer remember, using a package version that no longer exists, with a model endpoint
that has been deprecated.

--

<br>

I have watched colleagues lose weeks to this. It is entirely avoidable and entirely
self-inflicted.

---

# What happens in a review

You submit. A desk-reject filter runs first, editor decides whether it goes out at all.
A large share of submissions never reach a referee.

--

<br>

If it goes out: 2–3 referees, several months.

--

<br>

Outcomes: reject, major revision, minor revision. **Accept on first round essentially
never happens.** If someone tells you it did, they are rounding.

--

<br>

R&R is a good outcome. Treat it as one.

---

# Reading a referee report

The first read is emotional. Everyone's is.

--

<br>

<br>

.large2[Read it, close it, wait 48 hours, read it again.]

--

<br>

The second read is a different document. What felt like hostility is usually a
compressed, poorly-worded version of a legitimate concern.

---

# What referee reports actually contain

Three categories, and sorting them is the whole skill:

--

**Points where they are right.** Concede cleanly and fix. This is most of the report.

--

**Points where they misunderstood.** Usually your fault. You wrote it unclearly.
Clarify in the text, not just in the letter. If one referee misread it, readers will too.

--

**Points where they are wrong.** These exist. Push back with evidence, respectfully, and
do the analysis that demonstrates it rather than asserting it.

---

# Writing the response letter

- First person plural. "We."
- Reproduce each comment, then respond. **Every** point, including the small ones.
- Concede what is right, explicitly and without hedging: "The referee is correct."
- Push back with **evidence**, never with indignation
- Point to specifics: "Table 2, Column 3," not "our results"
- New material in the letter gets its own numbering (Table I, Figure II)

--

<br>

Open with brief thanks and a numbered summary of the main changes. The editor may read
only that summary. Make it do work.

---

# The two failure modes

**Defensive.** Explaining why every criticism is misguided. Reads as inability to take
criticism, which is the single most damaging impression you can leave with an editor.

--

<br>

**Obsequious.** "We are extremely grateful for the reviewer's brilliant insight." Every
paragraph. It signals that you have no independent judgment about your own paper.

--

<br>

The register you want is **collegial and matter-of-fact**. A competent person
responding to competent criticism. That is all.

---

# On unresolvable disagreements

Sometimes a referee wants something you genuinely cannot or should not do.

--

<br>

Say so. Explain why. Offer the closest feasible alternative and run it.

--

<br>

"We were unable to implement the reviewer's suggestion because \[specific reason\]. We
instead did \[X\], which addresses the underlying concern by \[Y\]."

--

<br>

Editors accept this constantly when the reasoning is concrete. They reject it when it
reads as evasion.

---

# Registered reports

Emerging format. You submit the **introduction, design, and analysis plan** before
collecting data.

--

<br>

Referees review the design. If accepted in principle, publication is **guaranteed
regardless of the result**.

--

<br>

This eliminates publication bias by construction, and it moves referee input to when it
can still improve the study rather than after it is too late.

--

<br>

Available at a growing set of journals, still rare in marketing. If you are running a
costly experiment, it is worth asking the editor.

---

# One piece of career advice

.large2[Referee. Early, and take it seriously.]

--

<br>

Nothing improves your own writing faster than reading twenty flawed papers carefully and
being forced to articulate exactly what is wrong.

--

<br>

You will start recognizing your own moves in other people's papers. That is unpleasant
and extremely useful.

---
class: inverse, center, middle
name: close

# Where this leaves you

---

# The through-line

Weeks 1–3: can anyone check what you did?

Weeks 4–5: does your variable measure what you claim?

Week 6: does your comparison identify what you claim?

--

<br>

<br>

.large2[All three have to hold. Any one of them failing makes the other two irrelevant.]

---

# The one thing to take from today

Cheap computation removed the friction that used to discipline empirical work.

--

<br>

It did not remove the need for the discipline.

--

<br>

.large2[The constraint has to come from **design and commitment** now, because it no
longer comes from cost.]

--

<br>

That is a harder problem than the one your advisors had, and you are the ones who have
to solve it.

---

# Week 6 milestone

Due before next class:

--

**1. Identification argument, written out.** One to two pages. It must answer the four
questions explicitly:

- What is the estimand?
- What is the identifying assumption?
- What would break it?
- What is the most damaging alternative explanation, stated in its strongest form?

--

**2. Robustness plan.** The checks you will run, each with the concern it addresses, and
what result would make you abandon the claim.

--

<br>

Commit both before you look at any further results. The commit timestamp is the point.

---

# Week 7: presentations

20 minutes, plus questions. Everyone presents. Everyone attends.

--

<br>

I will ask the four questions out loud. So will your classmates. That is the format.

---

# What a good presentation does

**Motivates the question** in two minutes. Not five. Why should anyone care, and what do
we not currently know?

--

**States the estimand and the identifying assumption** explicitly, on a slide, in words.

--

**Shows the validation.** Sampling scheme, confusion matrix, accuracy. This is your
instrument, establish it.

--

**Shows naive versus corrected.** Side by side. The gap is your contribution to the
audience's understanding of the method.

--

**Is honest about limits.** What you could not rule out, and what you would need to.

---

# What a bad presentation does

Spends twelve minutes on institutional background.

--

Shows a regression table and describes the coefficients out loud without interpreting
them.

--

Says "we validated the measure" without showing the validation.

--

Presents the corrected estimate only, so nobody can see what the correction did.

--

Claims more than the design supports and hopes nobody asks.

--

<br>

Someone will ask. In this room it will probably be me, but in three years it will be a
referee, and they will not be as friendly.

---

# Reading for next week

Nothing new. Finish your analysis and build your slides.

--

<br>

Come to office hours this week if:

- your effect is not there and you are not sure whether it is a precise zero
- your design has staggered adoption and you have not run the diagnostics
- you are unsure what your identifying assumption actually is

--

<br>

That last one is the most common and the most fixable. Come early.
